READING

**The financial structure of PENDLARROW**

The fit-out at £260,000 will consume most of the £310,000 on deposit regardless of which course is chosen. Under WESTERGATE the practice finishes with £50,000 in hand and no borrowing. Under PENDLARROW it must also buy a fitted vehicle at £34,000, leaving £16,000. That is a very thin operating reserve for a fifteen-person practice running two existing premises and opening a third, and the grant does not arrive until after the April 2027 assessment — roughly eighteen months after the builder's order date. The practice is therefore carrying the full fit-out cost plus the vehicle against a slender cash buffer for the best part of a year before any grant money returns.

**The Ardgowrie economics apart from the grant**

Revenue is £118,000. The dedicated vet costs £71,000 including on-costs, leaving £47,000 before vehicle depreciation. If the vehicle is capitalised over five years the annual charge is approximately £6,800, reducing the net contribution to around £40,000 a year. That is a reasonable return on the contract in isolation, but it is not a transformative one, and the question is whether the operational cost attached to it is adequately reflected in those figures.

**The grant eligibility calculation and its hidden risk**

The briefing states that adding Ardgowrie to last year's figures produces a farm-and-equine share of 31.8 per cent. The arithmetic is £622,000 against £1,958,000. What that calculation does is add £118,000 to the FY2026 total without adjusting the small animal line for growth in the period between the year ending March 2026 and the assessment date of April 2027 — a gap of thirteen months.

Small animal has grown at eleven per cent a year for four years. By April 2027 the annualised run rate for small animal work will be approximately £1,336,000 × (1.11)^(13/12), which is in the range of £1,495,000 to £1,500,000. The grant wording is "the annualised value of the work in force on that date." That phrase is not "the most recently filed accounts." It points to a current-state snapshot: what is the practice generating right now, expressed as an annual figure?

If the assessor uses a current run-rate measure for small animal — which the language invites — the denominator is approximately £622,000 + £1,498,000 = £2,120,000, and the farm-and-equine share is £622,000 / £2,120,000 = 29.3 per cent. That is below the thirty per cent floor. Even using the trailing twelve months to March 2027 (£1,483,000 for small animal) gives 29.6 per cent. On either of these readings the grant is not payable.

The only reading that produces 31.8 per cent and eligibility is one that uses FY2026 actual small animal revenue as a fixed base and then layers the new Ardgowrie contract on top — a mixed-methodology approach. Grant assessors may do exactly that (using the most recently completed audited accounts as the non-contractual baseline), but the practice cannot assume they will. This is a material ambiguity. Before an order is signed in October, the practice should put the methodology question to the grant authority in writing, because if the assessor applies a current run-rate to small animal, the entire financial rationale for PENDLARROW — the £100,000 offset against a £260,000 fit-out — disappears and the practice is left with the vehicle cost, the thin cash position, and all of the obligations described below.

**The night call-out load**

Ardgowrie's outgoing practice had the contract for nine years and gave it back in June. The reason they gave on the handover call was the night call-out load. This is the most specific and unambiguous piece of intelligence in the file. Nine years is long enough to rule out early teething problems; the practice was experienced with this herd and still found the call-out load untenable.

The load is structural, not circumstantial. Nine hundred dairy cattle have calving, mastitis, lameness and metabolic crises at night. That does not change with the change of practice. Kirstie Ballantyne-Rowe is willing to move with the contract, which is valuable continuity, but one farm vet cannot carry seven nights a week indefinitely — that is presumably part of what wore the previous arrangement down. The practice would need to build a farm night rota around her, recruiting into a role whose defining difficulty is the call-out pattern that just ended a nine-year relationship.

The practice is simultaneously opening Ordsall Green and is, on the evidence, fully occupying its management bandwidth with that project. Adding a farm night rota at the same moment is a compounding risk.

**The 2030 lock-in**

If the grant is paid, the practice must hold a herd health contract of 700 or more cattle until April 2030 or repay the full £100,000. That is not just a commitment to Ardgowrie; it is a commitment to maintaining the farm capability — the farm vet, the vehicle, the rota — even if the contract becomes operationally unsustainable, because the alternative is full repayment. The outgoing practice walked away from an arrangement it had held for nine years. If similar pressures built here, the practice would face a choice between continuing under strain or writing a £100,000 cheque.

**The small animal growth trajectory**

Small animal at eleven per cent compound over four years is a demonstrable trend, not a projection. The Ordsall Green surgery is a capacity investment against that trend, and it makes sense with or without Ardgowrie. The next hire under WESTERGATE goes into small animal, which is the segment actually growing. Under PENDLARROW the next hire is a farm vet whose salary is almost entirely absorbed by the Ardgowrie contract, and who brings with it the night rota obligation that constrained the previous holder.

**Weighing it**

PENDLARROW offers a £100,000 grant (uncertain on the qualification analysis above), a net annual contribution from Ardgowrie of approximately £40,000, and a strengthened rural profile. Against that: a cash reserve of £16,000 after fit-out and vehicle, grant eligibility dependent on a methodology the practice has not confirmed, a four-year repayment lock-in, and the night call-out load that is on the file as the documented reason this specific contract is available.

WESTERGATE costs £100,000 more in the short term and leaves £50,000 in reserve. It places the next hire where the growth is. It carries no overnight farm obligation and no lock-in. The farm-and-equine book stays flat, but it is already flat and there is no signal it will recover under any scenario.

The asymmetry is meaningful: if PENDLARROW works it saves £100,000 net of the vehicle and generates ~£40,000 a year at the cost of a night rota; if it goes wrong — whether because the grant fails, because the night load proves unsustainable, or because the practice needs to exit before 2030 — the downside is cash-tight operations, possible repayment, and the operational damage of a forced unwind during a period of expansion. WESTERGATE's downside is simply that the £100,000 forgone has to be earned back through the small animal growth that is already in the numbers.

---

READING
  The briefing's 31.8 per cent grant-qualification figure is calculated by adding the Ardgowrie contract to the FY2026 small animal base without adjusting for the eleven per cent annual small animal growth that will have occurred by the April 2027 assessment. Under a current-run-rate reading of "the annualised value of the work in force on that date" — which the grant wording supports — small animal would be approximately £1,498,000 and the farm-and-equine share falls to around 29.3 per cent, below the thirty per cent floor; even trailing twelve months to March 2027 gives 29.6 per cent. Eligibility is therefore genuinely uncertain and should be confirmed in writing with the grant authority before the October order is placed, because if the ratio fails the financial case for PENDLARROW collapses. Separately and independently, the outgoing practice surrendered this specific contract after nine years with night call-out load as the stated reason: the load is structural (900 dairy cattle do not change their calving patterns), Kirstie Ballantyne-Rowe cannot single-handedly carry it indefinitely, and the practice would be building a farm night rota during the same period it is opening Ordsall Green. Cash after fit-out and vehicle under PENDLARROW is £16,000, which is an inadequate buffer for a fifteen-person practice across three premises. The 2030 lock-in means the practice could not exit the cattle commitment even if it proved unsustainable without repaying £100,000 in full. WESTERGATE costs the £100,000 grant, leaves £50,000 in reserve, directs the next hire into the eleven-per-cent-growth segment, and carries none of the call-out or lock-in obligations. The forgone £100,000 is the whole downside; the upside of the small animal growth trajectory is already in evidence.

CALL
  WESTERGATE

GROUNDS
  The night call-out load that caused the previous holder to surrender this specific contract after nine years is structural, not circumstantial, and it would fall on a practice whose cash will be reduced to £16,000 after the fit-out and vehicle, whose grant eligibility is uncertain because small animal growth will likely push the farm-and-equine share below thirty per cent at the April 2027 assessment, and which is simultaneously establishing a new surgery at Ordsall Green.
